description: We are a team of passionate students driven by innovation, creativity, and problem-solving. With diverse technical skills and a collaborative mindset, we aim to use NASA’s open data and technology to develop practical solutions to real-world challenges. We look forward to learning, experimenting, and turning bold ideas into impactful solutions for Earth and space..
summary: CATALYX Mission Design Lab is a playable space mission design game for students and aspiring engineers. Players take a mission from idea to flight: they choose science goals, a launch vehicle and orbit, instruments, power, radio, pointing and propulsion, then fly the mission through random failures. Four scenarios (Landsat-style Earth observation, a lunar ice orbiter, a Mars relay orbiter and a Sun-Earth L2 space telescope) follow NASA's Concept Maturity Levels, and Mission Control can throw unexpected twists such as a budget cut. Every decision has a measurable consequence on mass, power, data, cost, schedule and reliability, shown live on a mission dashboard. One to four players can collaborate with different roles (Mission Lead, Launch and Ops, Spacecraft Engineer, Science and Comms) and must negotiate. After a launch countdown, the flight plays with live telemetry and a mid-mission decision of your own, then 300 simulated flights produce a score and a debrief that explains why the mission succeeded or failed. NASA data is integral: live DONKI space weather changes drag and radiation storms, and NASA's design methods and reference missions structure the game.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

CATALYX Mission Design Lab is a playable game in which students design, launch and debrief a complete space mission. The play loop follows NASA's Concept Maturity Levels: (1) Concept: choose science objectives and success criteria. (2) Architecture: run a launch-vehicle trade study and pick an orbit. (3) Point design: select instruments and size power, radio, pointing, propulsion, thermal control, redundancy and parts quality. (4) Ground and review: choose ground stations or Deep Space Network time and check margins. A live dashboard updates mass, power, data, link rate, delta-v, propellant, cost, schedule and reliability, and every red or amber check explains why it matters.

Under the sliders is a TypeScript engine with two-body orbital mechanics, the rocket equation to size propellant, an atmospheric-drag model, propagated ground-station contacts, a decibel link budget, eclipse and battery models, and a parametric cost and schedule model. Launching runs a narrated flight with live telemetry, then 300 Monte Carlo flights with launch failure, insertion risk, solar storms, micrometeoroids, instrument anomalies, ground outages and cost growth against the reserve. During the flight the player makes two real decisions: how to ride out a solar storm, and how to recover a faulted instrument. The score blends science return, engineering margins, cost efficiency, risk, and process/teamwork, and the debrief ranks the causes of any shortfall so the next design is better.

Four scenarios (Earth observation, lunar ice orbiter, Mars relay orbiter, Sun-Earth L2 space telescope) range from beginner to advanced. Each is benchmarked against a real mission (Landsat 9, LRO, MRO, JWST).

BENEFITS

Classes teach orbits, power and link budgets one formula at a time. Real missions are decided by how those numbers collide. In CATALYX one change, such as adding a 13 kg instrument, shows its consequences on mass, power, data, cost and schedule at once, and the player learns to trade them off. It is free, runs in any browser with no login, and has three difficulty levels and a sandbox. Teams can save, compare and share designs. A built-in Mission Coach tests about a hundred one-change variants of a player's design and explains which helps and why, so players learn from feedback instead of guessing.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want students and aspiring engineers to understand systems engineering, the idea that every spacecraft decision pulls on every other, before they ever meet it in a university course. The game builds teamwork and communication skills as well: up to four players take different roles (Mission Lead, Launch and Ops, Spacecraft Engineer, Science and Comms), each with a private priority, and must negotiate. Only the Lead can give the final go for launch. We hope it makes mission design feel approachable and encourages more students to consider careers in space.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js (3D spacecraft and orbit views), Zustand, PeerJS / WebRTC for peer-to-peer team rooms (optional Supabase Realtime), Vitest (36 physics, evaluation, simulation, coach and fuzz tests), and GitHub Pages for hosting. No special hardware is needed. A phone or laptop browser is enough. The orbit can be exported as a starter script for NASA's GMAT.

NASA DATA

Live NASA DONKI space-weather data (coronal mass ejections and geomagnetic storms) sets a solar-activity factor in every flight, so real conditions change drag and radiation risk. The mission structure uses NASA Concept Maturity Levels and the Mission Design Lab process. Earth imagery is NASA Blue Marble, and the L2 telescope's targets come from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Launcher specifications are approximated from public ISRO, ESA and JAXA data.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of a quiz or a calculator, the project turns real engineering trade-offs into a game with consequences. The player sees what a choice costs before making it, through what-if previews and live change indicators. They feel the risk by watching a flight that can fail, and they own it through in-flight decisions with no safe answer. The crew mode forces the kind of negotiation real mission teams have. A daily challenge with streaks, 14 badges, random Mission Control twists such as a sudden budget cut, a leaderboard and shareable design links give players a reason to come back.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy versus approachability: the numbers are rounded educational approximations of public references, not mission-planning data, and we say so in the app. Accessibility: free, browser-based, no login, works on phones. Learning value: every warning explains why it matters, and the debrief explains why the mission succeeded or failed. Collaboration: it works across devices without a server. Reliability: seeded random streams keep all players in a room on the identical flight, and automated tests guard the physics. Honest limits: the GMAT export follows the documented script language but has not yet been run inside GMAT.
